title: Googlebook Shows Promise, but Not Quite Ready
body:
It’s 2026, and Google has introduced Googlebooks, a new companion for your Android phone. There aren’t any budget Googlebooks available at the moment, and the Lenovo is no exception. The hardware is nice, featuring an attractive design headlined by a beautiful 3K OLED display running at 120Hz. It has an oversized haptic trackpad, 16GB of memory, and is one of the lightest 15” laptops I’ve ever held. Unfortunately, it’s also expensive, and doesn’t have a higher-end CPU to match its price.

The software is entirely new. It’s Android for the desktop, now called Googlebook OS. The operating system itself is refreshing to use, especially if you enjoy the experience on Google’s latest Pixel devices. In fact, it nearly looks identical, right down to a lot of the same settings. There are even leftover phone artifacts such as options for a mobile hotspot, despite the laptop not having a cellular modem, and options to turn on “Data Saver”.

One of the big selling points of a Googlebook is the deep integration with your Android phone. You can cast apps from your phone to the desktop, interact with your notifications, and manage files or photos on your phone. In practice, however, I found these features didn’t always work particularly well. A lot of times casting wouldn’t work, and I’d be prompted to scan a QR code to re-pair my Pixel phone to the laptop. Notifications were inconsistent, sometimes appearing and sometimes not. Even when they did appear, interacting with them did not always work. Reddit, for example, would send a notification from my phone, but clicking on it would simply cause my phone’s screen to light up as it attempted to cast the application. Then ultimately nothing happened, likely because I didn’t have Reddit installed on the Googlebook. Worse, the notification would then disappear from both devices.

Performance has been just ok. The laptop feels snappy for the most part, but looking at the included CPU and running some benchmarks, it’s not substantially more powerful than my Google Pixel Pro 11. It also has the same amount of memory. Considering that it runs many of the same apps, likely at a similar speed, the primary advantages over my phone are the larger display, included keyboard, and trackpad.

Battery life has been outstanding. This was a surprise to me because the laptop uses an Intel processor, rather than an ARM-based Snapdragon chip. Combined with the lightweight design, this is easily one of the biggest selling points for this laptop. 

Installing apps involves visiting the Play Store, just as you would on an Android phone. There are now labels in the Play Store that indicate whether an app is compatible, “Optimized for Desktop”, or “Made for Desktop”. The latter should provide the best experience, but unfortunately, there are very few of these available. Most first-party apps such as Chrome are “made for desktop”, along with a lot of image editors like Canva. However, many still feel like web apps originally designed with ChromeOS in mind. Even Chrome has issues. For example, video on some websites would play at a very poor framerate (although Youtube works fine, it’s a Google product after all)

A lot of apps are “optimized” but that doesn’t mean they’re fully featured desktop applications. It typically means the interface is responsive and scales appropriately and that it supports the built-in keyboard and trackpad. Microsoft Word, an “optimized” app, is a perfect example. The experience is surprisingly poor, which is particularly disappointing considering writing documents for school or work would be one of the primary reasons to use a Googlebook.

In fact, I wrote this review in Word on the Googlebook. The experience was a bit frustrating. I could not select text normally or copy/paste with the regular keyboard shortcuts. Typing would lag at times, while strange graphical artifacts would be visible from time to time. The application’s functionality itself is stripped down compared to the desktop version on Mac or Windows. Honestly, it’s so bad you just want to pull out a real laptop to get work done.

I was particularly excited about the built-in Linux environment, thinking that I could install anything through the terminal that I couldn’t find in the Play Store. Apps such as VS Code and Gimp would provide me with some familiarity for development and photo editing. Unfortunately, at this time, Linux feels like a second-class citizen, at best used for CLI only commands. While I managed to get both installed, I could not get Code to run and Gimp had a lot UI interface issues. If you do want to code, Google's Antigravity app works if that’s what you’re comfortable using.

The speakers are better than I expected. They could use a bit more bass response but for the most part they work well.

Another area where the Googlebook excels is the Gemini experience. Google’s flagship AI is integrated directly into the operating system, with features like Magic Pointer, which lets you interact with anything on your screen and Rambler, which is smart AI dictation and my favorite feature from this year's Pixel phones. You can also create custom desktop widgets using natural language. If you’re heavily invested in Gemini and Google’s AI features, there’s definitely something to appreciate here.

Pros:
- Extremely lightweight premium design
- Gorgeous 3K OLED 120Hz Display
- App-casting from Android phone
- Good multi-monitor support
- Great sounding speakers
- Built-in Gemini integration
- Instant on functionality
- Excellent battery life
- Large haptic Trackpad
- Linux Support
- Biometric login
- Thunderbolt 4 and Wifi 7
- Includes 1 year of Google AI Pro

Cons:
- Midrange CPU and integrated graphics
- Limited desktop ecosystem for Android
- Early Adopter Bugs – like keyboard lag and inconsistent phone integration
- Linux is mostly limited to CLI terminal emulator
- Expensive

Overall – I find myself enjoying the Googlebook and while simultaneously wondering if I could ever actually use it as my primary device. The hardware is excellent, battery life is fantastic, and Googlebook OS is different and refreshing to use. But it all comes down to the apps. While casual users may find everything they need, the lack of true desktop apps at this early stage of the products lifecycle can make the experience frustrating for all but the most dedicated Android enthusiasts. With more time and especially developer support this could be a true competitor to Mac and Windows based systems.

title: Nice hardware but missed opportunity
body:
Title: Nice hardware but missed opportunity

Verdict: The Lenovo Googlebook is a beautiful computer with decent specs and great Google ecosystem integration. However, it lacks the ability to run real programs and the AI features were disappointing. I would recommend this to users heavily invested in the Google ecosystem and that do not have a requirement for heavy programs.

First impressions. I like the white laptop. It’s a nice size, but it’s not heavy. Cool startup logo! 

Setup. You can setup from an iPad or Android device, so probably mobile first approach. During initial setup, you can opt out of signing into a Google account. The computer will provide options to setup fingerprint unlock and/or face unlock, both of which work quite well.
- Setup without an account: If you select this option, a warning box will advise that you will not have access to seamless Google services until you sign in. From there you can add your name and essentially setup a permanent local account. I tried this to see how it worked, and essentially, this computer is mostly a browser if it doesn’t include you Google sign-in (access to sheets, doc, or other Google product requires sign-in).

- Setup with an account: Definitely the way to go. Once you get to your desktop, you can get to all your Google data: email app to your Gmail, files in Google Drive, all your Chrome history, Youtube account, etc. Fundamentally, I think this is the best way to use this computer for one or several users. This way, any user that logs in will immediately have all of their Google account, tools, and data available.

Usage. I love that there is a tutorial video as soon as the laptop loads. However… the video demos are too small! I can barely read what’s in the video, yet half the screen on my computer is white space!! That doesn’t make sense. Coming from an exclusive Windows computer experience, there is definitely a small learning curve… There seems to be no right click, and I keep trying because it’s faster and makes sense to me, for example removing Drop Box from the taskbar… Can’t right click to do that with the touchpad and nearly impossible to figure out how to remove it (had to Google it! And it’s clicking with two fingers at once…). However, when you add a physical mouse (or BT mouse), you can instantly right click and remove it… I don’t understand why not just keep right click on the touchpad to ease the transition from Windows.

Power users. Since we are heavily invested in Google workspace, appsheet tools, scripts, etc., I have been wondering if we could switch to using these at work. It appears that you can still load something like Microsoft Office through the Google store (must have for us to execute advanced formatting). Adobe Acrobat just had the reader; I could not find the pro version. An Adobe Acrobat browser plugin does exist for Chrome but it’s not the same thing. I think we could switch some users because they use mostly web-based apps, but other users need installed programs. 

AI Tools. Access to Gemini pro and Nano Banana for a year is a very nice perk that sweetens the deal. 

Things I love:
- Nice Lenovo hardware
- Beautiful 3K OLED screen
- Good-looking laptop, and it feels really nice
- Super lightweight for its size
- Performs better than its specs
- Security and anti-virus built-in
- Decent specs
- Thank you for the privacy shutter!

Things I don’t like:
- The black bar at the top of the screen takes away from screen real-estate. I understand that they want to give the ecosystem a mobile vibe, but that is so impractical and counter-productive. Put the time, date, and WiFi, and notifications back in the task bar so I can get some real-estate back
- I was interested to try Magic Pointer but it doesn’t work for me… I can’t turn it on.
- I was disappointed with the Built-In Gemini. It’s not really on par with another AI you download and it can use tools such as the web browser  to check things for you.

Overall, this is a nice start for this Googlebook by Lenovo… Nice hardware and very nice integration with the Google ecosystem. However, I think it could be so much more by fully empowering Gemini and AI tool use on the laptop, and more real programs for power users. I would recommend this to users heavily invested in the Google ecosystem and that do not have a requirement for heavy programs.

title: Gorgeous, But Held Back Slightly by Early Quirks
body:
I want to completely love this laptop, and most days I think I do. It solves my portability needs beautifully. The sleek Cloud Grey metal chassis has a surprisingly soft-to-the-touch feel, and its lightweight design makes it effortless to carry around, which is a massive win for someone with hand dexterity issues. The 3K OLED screen is gorgeous, and the Gemini AI integration is fantastic and lightning-fast.

However, the occasional software and connection hiccups keep it from absolute perfection. One of the main reasons I purchased this was for seamless continuity with my phone. While it works wonderfully when it cooperates, the connection can be hit-or-miss and laggy at times, forcing me to manually reconnect. Additionally, powered by Intel, it handles day-to-day tasks fine, but it does feel a bit less snappy compared to Snapdragon-powered alternatives I’ve tested.

As for all the not-so-positive reviews the Lenovo is getting, that's not a thing for me. My comments are based on my own empirical observations. I expect some wrinkles, and I believe they are going to be worked out. My suggestion is just to try it and see if it works for you.

Overall, it's a "soft" 4 stars because the hardware fundamentals and portability are just that good. Because I purchased it with a Best Buy Total Membership Protection Plan, I have peace of mind and some time to see if future updates iron out these early wrinkles.

title: Great Hardware, software is not there yet.
body:
Here we go again!  I decided to be a beta tester for Google.  I purchased a Googlebook.  I actually purchased the Acer Googlebook first.  I liked the Hardware mostly, but had issues with my phone not connecting.  I did not go into deep troubleshooting because I was turned off by the amount of fingerprints on the blue finish in just a short amount of time.  As I said, very nice hardware minus the fingerprint part, but I returned it. I got the Lenovo version.

For $1099 I considered the price still fair based on the specs.  I did get a Lenovo Chromebook Plus 14 prior and for a mere $541 open box.  With the Chromebook the OLED screen is beautiful and very responsive.  It is a great all arounder, and if you can find it for <$700, I highly recommend it.  

Back to the Lenovo Googlebook.  I really loved the magnesium alloy material and how it had a soft touch. The white color was really nice.  For a larger laptop it is amazingly light. For comparison it weighs almost the same amount as the 14 inch Chromebook Plus model.  My only issue with the hardware is that the haptic touchpad on my model had a sort of hollow rattle on one corner, which is odd for a haptic touchpad. 

I was also pleasantly surprised by the display as I normally am more into glossy displays.  This one is anti-glare.and with the high resolution gives the images a soft yet sharp look.   Using the laptop with 120hz does not feel all that special as the Chromebook Plus 14 scrolls the page faster.  The googlebooks are not the only ones that are guilty of this as the Surface Laptop 7 I had was the same when using the touchpad to scroll.  The Surface Pro does not have this issue in either touch or trackpad use.  Weirdly the Chromebook one scrolls significantly faster despite the 60hz. 

I tried so much with this laptop to make it work, but I had the same issue that my phone would not remain paired.  This is the reason I wanted a googlebook.  I like having a laptop that does not have the bloat of windows and I want to use it unlike MacOS.  The question for me isn't who are Googlebooks for, but rather why does it not work consistently with pairing like my car does with AA when I get in.  The brief time it worked right it was nice having my phone's apps visible and all the android apps installed.  It felt like an extension of my phone.  That is all I want.  No complicated OS just browsing and using connected apps. 

Right now I would wait on Googlebooks to get more reliable software to work the way they are advertised to.  The Lenovo Chromebook 14 Plus works more reliably than the Googlebook so there is work to be done here.

title: On the right track!
body:
When I heard about the Googlebooks coming out, I got excited. “This is what I’ve been waiting for - for a very long time” I exclaimed! I've tried Chromebooks before and I just don't like Chrome OS. A big blank home screen or desktop just doesn't seem very productive. I love Android. The ability to have the widgets that you want and have folders right on your desktop is what I've been looking for without being a Windows machine. So I definitely wanted to get the Lenovo Googlebook.
So far trying this out, there are some good things and some not so good things. It definitely isn't fully baked yet, but if you like seeing how technology progresses, it's kind of neat to get it now and see how they'll improve it. Think of it like a prototype.
The overall build quality is so-so for me right away. I love that it's nice and light, but the coating that they use on the outside that makes it so nice and smooth, I wish it had a little bit more texture so it's a little more grippy. Being so smooth and whatever the coating is, it actually makes the "premium" magnesium/aluminium blend feel like plastic. If you tap your fingers on the underside of it or on the cover, I swear it's plastic. I like the little tab running across the top. When it's closed, it makes it so easy to open this with one finger. I don't really understand the glow bar on the back of the screen facing away from you. Among other things I thought it was supposed to show the battery charge, but while it's charging up, the glow bar is off. It does not show any kind of level. Hopefully, that is definitely something they add more features to, to make it have a point.
I like the Lenovo Googlebook due to its size. I love the big screen. It gets nice and bright and nice and dim in dark environments. The screen is beautiful. It has an amazing picture, very vibrant and a responsive touchscreen. Also, the face unlock works great as long as you're in a bright room, but in the morning when it's dark and I try to open it, it does not work at all. I always have to put my pin in. The bigger size gives you a well-spaced out keyboard. It's easier to type on. Key travel and clickiness is very nice. Love the fact that it's backlit and easily adjustable. The big trackpad is nice, but I think this could use some work. The haptics on it don't feel premium; it feels a little hollow and kind of cheapy. One and two fingers on it is great, but the three finger gestures I don't care for. It's awkward to try to use those. It should just have the same swipe gestures as the screen can have. It's nice to have a fingerprint reader right on the keyboard, but it is very slow. 
The battery life is pretty good. I use my laptop for my admin every morning for a couple hours and I get just about four days out of it before I have to recharge it. If I were to use it all in one time, I'd probably get about nine to ten hours out of it. When you close the lid and it goes into sleep mode, that's nice, it only loses about 6 to 7% of battery life. Recharging it is pretty quick; I plug it in and it charges up in about an hour and 20 minutes from 15%.
When it comes to actually using the Google Book and the experience, I would say it's mostly positive with a few annoyances that hopefully Google will be fixing with updates. I would have liked to have seen more updates during the about a week I've had it, but I haven't seen anything come through yet. 
Setting up the Googlebook was just like setting up an Android phone, that went super easy. Most apps went over, there's only a few that I had to go and download. But here is the first annoyance, that this is running Android 17 but it doesn't run all Android apps. Some of the main ones like YouTube and Gmail are still progressive web apps or PWAs, and I don't like those. That's what they use on Chrome OS. I want the Android apps. Google absolutely needs to fix this. Continue on seems to work pretty well, although I had to go into my Pixel phone and turn on the feature because it wasn't on right away. But it is really nice to be able to be browsing the web on your phone and think, "Oh, I want to see this bigger," and just go right to the laptop. 
The cast apps feature is bad. It's a great thought but it needs a lot of work. When I try to use it, the apps will come up but there will be missing elements, big blank spaces, or they're just very jittery and unusable. 
The Googlebooks come with Rambler baked in and that is one of my favorite features ever. I use it all the time and it needs to be made available for any electronic device used for communication. It is just so great!
The notifications on the Googlebook need a lot of work as well. I will get double notifications, or I will get notifications that pop up every time I start using it in the morning that I have dismissed hours ago. As long as you're using the Googlebook and your phone together, you can swipe the notifications away, but done separately, the Googlebook has to play catch up.
There is only one volume, (which was I think a thing back in the early 2000s). Come on Google, what happened to the separate volumes for notifications and media and alarms? I hate having the volume up louder when I'm watching something or listening to music and then later a notification will come through blaring loud. I've had to shut them off until they get that fixed.
Casting from the Googlebook to other devices like your TV isn't a great experience. It only finds specifically Google products. If I try to cast something from my Pixel phone, it will show all the Google things and my Fire Sticks and all my devices that I can cast to.

For about a week, I have tried to exclusively use this Lenovo Googlebook and leave my tablet on the table and see if it can replace it, and so far it has been able to. I have some preferences for the tablet, but if Google pushes out updates and fixes these issues, it will absolutely be a wonderful machine.

title: Fresh Laptop Experience
body:
I've used plenty of laptops over the years, and the Lenovo Googlebook 15 immediately felt different in a good way. This isn't replacing my main computer, but it has quickly become a device I genuinely enjoy picking up for everyday use.
 The first thing that stood out was how incredibly light it feels for a 15.3-inch laptop. It's easy to carry around the house, use on the couch, or throw into a bag for travel without feeling like i'm hauling around a large-screen notebook. The size-to-weight ratio is really impressive.
 The second thing I noticed was the haptic touchpad. Instead of a traditional physical click, Lenovo uses a haptic system that provides feedback electronically. It feels smooth, modern, and surprisingly premium. After using it for a while, going back to a traditional clickpad feels a bit dated. The touchpad alone gives the laptop a very polished feel.
 The 15.3-inch OLED display is another highlight. Colors are vibrant, blacks are deep, and the 120Hz refresh rate makes scrolling and navigation feel fluid. I was surprised while i was using the Youtube app it was giving me the option to watch content in 8K which by the way it was very impressive!
 Lenovo pairs that gorgeous display with a great set of speakers (dolby atmos) and that's a wining combination, in my opinion adds to the already Premium feeling of this laptop. 
 Bottom Line:

title: Excellent Build Quality
body:
I think Lenovo built the best looking Googlebook and sitting it next to my Lenovo Chromebook Plus, its the exact same design, with a color shade difference. Lately it seems the design of laptops makes it hard to actually use on the lap, as the fans pull from the bottom and right where they would sit on the lap.. Lenovo’s fan placement is technically pulls from the bottom. I’ve seen a lot of reviewers saying that the Lenovo Googlebook 15 doesn’t have fans. Not too sure they paid close enough to detail. Especially since this is a reused design.

Overall the build quality is excellent! Extremely light and sturdy. There is minimal chassis flex. There are three components of the chassis: lid, base, and input shell. The base is a poly-carbonate with wave design. The lid is magnesium-aluminum and the input shell is magnesium-carbon fiber. Each surface is painted with a fingerprint free eggshell finish.

 Weight is 2.84lbs (1.29kg) and it is extremely well balanced.

Lenovo’s is the largest of the new Googlebook lineup and offers an awesome 15.3 inch OLED screen perfect for running multiple windows or binge watching some shows.

Audio is excellent for a laptop and having the up-firing speakers helps not to muffle the sound. Thankfully it has a headphone port and a host of others that also make this version of the Googlebook standout. Either of the USB-C ports can be used for charging or 10GB/s data transfer. And that still leaves a USB-A 3.2 and an HDMI port.

The keyboard is nice, the keys are a little louder than I would like, not quite a mechanical keyboard decibel, but has the press satisfaction of a solid keyboard. I don’t know if it is the trackpad size, but the palm rejection definitely needs some updating. Since that is the software side, I don’t know if that will come through GoogleOS or or driver support? Specs say it has haptic feedback, but I don’t feel that come through.

As a laptop I love it. But this isn’t just another laptop.

GoogleOS based on AndroidOS, which operates similarly to Android Desktop, with a little ChromeOS still shining through.

GoogleOS feels like a gooey brownie you're trying to cook through but not over do it and you just stuck the toothpick in the for the first time…and its still got some batter on it.

Even though there is a familiarity with the OS coming from Android phones it really helps if you are a Pixel user or at least an Android that doesn’t use its own skin/launcher, there is still a learning curve, as this is not just a straight port of Android or even Android Desktop experience.

Comparing it to ChromeOS, I definitely like the direction Google is going, as this feels like a real OS meant for getting things done. As stated the brownies aren’t done yet, but they will be with some time. Thankfully, though, in this situation, you can have your cake (brownie) and eat it too as out-of-the-box the OS is very usable and useful.

A lot of tech reviewers were riding these hard and understandably so, as the these are priced higher than a Chromebook Plus with the same specs and in some cases higher than a WindowsOS laptop, so the expectations are high and the results didn’t quite match. 

However, I think because there is a lot of familiarity with the OS because of ChromeOS and AndroidOS there were too many assumptions that it is the same or mild iteration with  just a keyboard attached to a massive screen.

But multiple, resizable windows are a massive jump from static windows on comparatively tiny screens.

As a business user, creator, and multiple Chrome Profile aficionado, I don’t know if a Googlebook can be my main laptop yet, but it definitely feels closer than ever.

title: The lightweight that hits like a heavyweight!
body:
The new Lenovo Googlebook 15.3" 3K 120Hz OLED Touchscreen Laptop features at the heart of its technology, Google's A.I.  and its excellent screen which uses OLED technology.  OLED stands for Organic Light Emitting Diodes.  I am a retired Electronics Technician with 39 years of experience and as such I will explain some features and acronyms to help show you how they benefit this Lenovo and you, the user.


Superior Image Quality -

Deep Blacks: OLED displays can turn off individual pixels, resulting in true black levels.

Vibrant Colors: The technology supports a wider color range, providing more vivid and lifelike images 
shown on-screen.

High Contrast Ratios: This is the ability to control brightness at the pixel level leads to exceptional contrast.

Lower Power Consumption -

Energy Efficiency: OLED screens consume less power, especially when displaying dark images, as they do not require backlighting.  This can also result in longer run times off the battery but it is  dependent upon what you are doing with the laptop and how much power is needed to perform any task(s).

Design -

Thin and Lightweight: OLED displays can be made thinner than traditional LCDs, allowing for more compact  device designs, which in turn can translate into less weight.

Another  advantage is that of faster response times in "drawing" the moving images onto the screen.  This feature reduces motion blur, and along with faster refresh rates such as the 120 Hz refresh rate of this Lenovo helps to make OLED displays ideal for gaming and fast-paced content.

During initial setup you can set things so you can speak to the A.I. or to leave that feature offline as I did and make your questions via the keypad.  The Screen is  as I said, an OLED with a refresh rate of 120 Hz which is suitable for viewing streaming movies with excellent fast-paced visuals and in my case zero motion stuttering during movies with high speed scenes and online live Hockey games.  In a word:  Excellent!

Upon completion of all updates, which took far less time than any Windows or iOS device in recent memory, I then went to the Google Store and downloaded the applications for Prime Music and Video as well as HBO-Max with the intent to use this laptop for listening to music and viewing movies/shows in bed at home or in a hotel when I travel.  I will later add Pandora and SiriusXM to the Lenovo.  I will say that the Lenovo Googlebook 15.3" 3K 120Hz OLED Touchscreen Laptop is perhaps the lightest, easiest and by far the most powerful Google device I have tested and used to date.  It is a lightweight with the power of a heavyweight!   I am  a senior citizen and I can say that I easily walked around our home carrying the Lenovo and was never fatigued nor did I ever drop the laptop.  That is a big deal to me.  The Lenovo Googlebook 15.3" 3K 120Hz OLED Touchscreen Laptop is perhaps the perfect travel laptop to stay in touch, stream movies and more.  I say this because of its excellent screen, superb speed and ease of use.  I recommend it to anyone that wants a simple, easy to use and easy to carry laptop!  Well done indeed, Lenovo!

title: Great display, some hardware and battery issues
body:
I do most of my daily writing and work in Google Docs and Sheets, and I already use Gemini Advanced, so a dedicated Google laptop made sense to try. It’s very portable and easy to take on the go, but at $1,100 there are definite compromises.

​The screen is easily the best part. Lenovo has really set the bar here. Most laptops in this price range come standard  with1200p or 1440p IPS panels, so getting a 15.3-inch 3K 120Hz OLED is great at $1,100. Text is sharp, colors pop, and glare hasn't been an issue at all. It's plenty bright, too. I usually leave it around 80% because anything higher hurts my eyes indoors.
​
Build-wise, it feels a little cheap and plasticky for the price tag. Under 2.9 lbs is nice, and it stays cool. I can let this sit on my lap for hours without it ever getting warm. But, there is obvious flex if you press the plastic strip between the function keys and the display. It doesn't feel solid.

​Now that I've spent substantial time typing on it, the keyboard is responsive, comfortable, and great for long typing sessions. The only real headache is a dumb design oversight with the backlighting: in a lit room, turning the backlight on completely washes out the lettering on the grey keys. You actually have to turn the backlight off in a lit room so the dark font contrast shows up. The trackpad is solid. The click feels reassuring, two-finger right-click works fine, and the fingerprint reader is instant if Face Unlock misses.

​Speakers are clear for speech and videos, but if you crank the volume, the bass distorts on drum hits. Plan on headphones.

​Performance is a mixed bag. Browser tabs and Gemini run fine, but opening actual apps feels sluggish—even with the Core Ultra 5, it just isn't as snappy as you'd expect. Battery life also hasn't been great, and I've noticed the percentage drops noticeably even just sitting with the lid shut. (Also worth noting: if you have an iPhone, pairing gives you basic text notifications, but that's about it.)

​I still need my desktop for local stuff like gaming and Roon, but for taking to work to have a dedicated Google app computer, it does the job. Strengths: Keyboard is great to type on. Display is excellent. Stays nice and cool. Weakness: Battery life. Backlit keyboard. Not as snappy as I'd like.

title: Amazing hardware, beta software, but still a buy!
body:
I've been using the Lenovo Googlebook 15 for about five days now, and I have to say, this is probably the nicest hardware I've used on a Google-based laptop. It's not a Chromebook, but I think Chromebook users are exactly the kind of people who are going to appreciate what Google is trying to do here. The hardware is absolutely gorgeous, but man, Google has some work to do on the software side.

First off, as far as the hardware goes, the laptop is a stunner. The Cloud Grey finish is awesome, and it's ridiculously light for a 15-inch laptop. The finish has this really smooth matte feel to it, and while it doesn't quite feel like the aluminum on a MacBook Air, it definitely doesn't feel cheap or plasticky either. I've mostly been using it at my desk but I'm actually excited to take this thing on the road because of how light it is.

The keyboard is good, although the keys are a little smaller than I'd like. Took me a little bit to adjust but nothing major. The trackpad though? Holy crap. It's huge, responsive, and easily one of the best I've ever used on a laptop. Seriously, it's that good.

And the screen. Wow. The 3K OLED display is just beautiful. Everything is incredibly sharp, especially text, which sounds like a weird thing to get excited about but it's one of the first things I noticed. I've been keeping the brightness around 80% and that's plenty for indoor use. It's not one of those displays where turning it up to 100% feels like it's going to burn your eyes out, but it's plenty bright. I haven’t used it in sunlight yet, so I do have some concerns that the 500 nits might limit where you can use it.   I’m also not normally a big touchscreen user because I hate getting fingerprints all over my screen, but for some reason I've been using this one quite a bit. And the anti-fingerprint coating seems to actually work because I'm not seeing nearly as many smudges as I'd expect. 

Performance has been great. Most of my work flow has been in Chrome and I've had plenty of.    tabs open, bounced between apps and haven't noticed any slowdown whatsoever. The Core Ultra 5 and 16GB of RAM seem like more than enough for what I'm doing, although I'm not exactly pushing this thing to its limits. I've also been playing games through the free GeForce NOW trial and that's worked really well, but obviously the heavy lifting is being done in the cloud, not on the laptop itself.

One thing that surprised me was the speakers. I've been listening to music while working and my normal mix sounds really good. Full, clear, and much better than I'd expect from something this thin. Gaming sounds great too. No, it's not going to replace a good set of speakers but for a laptop this light, I'm impressed.

Now let's talk about Googlebook OS because this is where things get interesting.
It's Android. I mean, there's really no other way to describe it. It's Android dressed up for a laptop, right down to the control panel and the way apps behave. Coming from a Chromebook, the experience is pretty familiar and all the Google stuff works great. Chrome, Docs, Sheets, Drive, no issues at all. If that's primarily what you use your computer for, you're going to be happy.

But the Android apps? Good lord.

Google has these different classifications in the Play Store telling you whether an app is made for desktop, optimized for desktop, compatible with desktop, etc. Sounds great in theory, but in practice some of those labels are a joke.

Take Microsoft Outlook. It's supposedly optimized for desktop, but trying to edit an email is maddening. Instead of being able to highlight text normally with the trackpad, it brings up those stupid little Android selection handles like you're typing on your phone. Excel has similar issues. I have this beautiful 15-inch display, a fantastic keyboard and probably the best trackpad I've used in years, and I'm sitting here tapping on the screen just to select a few cells? Come on.

I was also pretty excited to play Call of Duty Mobile since I play it on my Android tablets all the time. Nope. Doesn't work. I'm not sure if that's an Intel processor compatibility thing or what, but it's disappointing.

And that's my biggest frustration with this laptop. You have all these Android apps available, but so many of them still behave like phone apps even when Google says they're optimized for desktop. It really shows how fragmented the Android ecosystem still is. Hopefully developers get on board because right now this part of the experience feels half-baked.

The Pixel phone integration is pretty cool though. Setup was a little more involved than I expected, with QR codes and messing around in settings, but once it's connected it works quickly. Being able to open something like my banking app or a travel booking app without having to log into everything again is actually pretty handy. It's not quite as seamless as Apple's setup process, but it works.

A couple of little things worth mentioning. The webcam is fine, nothing special, but the little privacy slider is chintzy. It feels like I'm going to accidentally slide it right out of the laptop, and half the time I can't even tell if it's open or closed. Weirdly cheap feeling on an otherwise premium piece of hardware.
Battery life is something I'm still figuring out. I haven't run it down to zero yet, but I did notice it dropped from 100% to 78% after about 15 minutes of cloud gaming and some light browsing. That seems like a pretty quick drop to me, although I haven't used it long enough to make a real judgment there. At least it stays cool and quiet. I haven't noticed any heat or fan noise so far.

So why am I giving it five stars?

Because if you've been using Chromebooks for years and are tired of feeling like you're playing with a toy, this thing is a huge step in the right direction. Lenovo absolutely nailed the hardware. It's beautiful, lightweight, fast, and the screen and trackpad are fantastic.

But I wouldn't buy this expecting everything to work perfectly today. The Google apps are great, but third-party Android app compatibility needs a LOT of work. And honestly, the whole experience feels a little like Google released a beta version and decided to let the rest of us figure out what works.

title: Disappointed
body:
Having used Android tablets and Chromebooks for many years, I was very excited about getting a device that would give me the immediate functionality of a tablet combined with a laptop worthy file system. I had high hopes for Googlebook OS, but I must report my experience with the Lenovo Googlebook 15.

First of all, I state emphatically that this is a technological beauty. This device is sleek, wonderful to touch, and remarkably light for its screen size. Every aspect of the laptop is superb; gorgeous OLED display, wonderful trackpad, and one of the best keyboards I have ever used. Speakers are loud and clear. The only mechanical snags I have encountered are imperfect face recognition and fingerprint detection. (These work only a portion of the time.) 

The disappointment comes with the software experience. Since Googlebook OS was built on Android, I just figured that all of the apps on the Google Play Store would run, recognizing that only some apps would render well. However, I have found many apps that will not even open. Some of this might be due to the X86 processor. For example, Microsoft Edge browser for Android that works well on tablets will not open on the Lenovo. However, if one casts from a phone (I have a Pixel 10), I can run the Edge browser from my phone. It works, but is slow and sloppy. I have also tried to install Edge for Linux. This is a bit complicated, but it is possible to do. However, the browser is nearly unusable in that form. Applications that are run via the Linux terminal do not show up on the task bar, so there is no way to access them once they are downloaded except through the terminal. 

It is indeed wonderful to have a proper file system finally. I can add any number of cloud services to the file manager and access these sources easily. This is huge, and is probably the best improvement that Googlebook OS represents. There is improved window management as well, but this is quite imperfect. For instance, one cannot double-tap and drag a window; moving things around is best done with a mouse. I am also annoyed that when running multiple desktops one cannot move applications from one to another. It is also not possible to run multiple iterations of any application, including the Chrome browser. 

To top it all off, there appears to be no option for creating Progressive Web Apps from the Chrome browser. This is an inexcusable deficiency in my opinion. 

Bottom line: The Lenovo Googlebook 15 is a beautiful piece of hardware, but Googlebook OS prevents it from being a useful computer for me. An Android tablet runs Android applications better, a Chromebook runs Chrome better, and the Linux capabilities are severely limited.

title: Fast & useful, but not comfortable
body:
This is technically my second chromebook, but it feels like my first. I have a first gen chromebook from over 10 years ago that is still going with no issue. This years’ chromebook feels night and day different. This year's model is equipped with enough ports for any user. There are a couple of usb-C ports, 1 usb & hdmi. Also a finger print scanner that is obviously new from first gen for me. 
The OLED touch screen is great for me. Very responsive and easy to use. The picture looks really good. Movies and websites looked great too. This unit comes with a 65 watt charger that plugs into either of the C ports, which everyone chromebook and laptop maker needs to copy asap! The cable charged the chromebook pretty fast in my experience, plus now I have a back up quick charging cable I can use for my phone, for example, I love that! I have not used the battery to 0% for that test as of yet. Make sure you set the battery setting to 80% to keep it in the best shape. Annoying? Very, but in a few years, the battery should still be holding a full charge just as well with minimal degradation to the cells. .  
I want to bring up an annoying negative I have found out. The touchpad. First the positives: the click function feels unique with its rumble feature when pressing, and intuitive to use while gesturing or using as a normal mouse. The gestures were also easy to implement right away. Responsive to everything I tried out, 1, 2, or 3 button clicks were great use. The bad part is the keypad is just too large and sits too close to the keyboard. The issue arose when my hand was slightly touching the touchpad while typing, inadvertently moving the cursor to another line all together. 
As always, I want to be as fair as possible and state that not only do I use an ergonomic KB normally, I use the wrist rest it comes with when typing. With this chromebook, it feels like my typing posture went to boot camp.There is no slouching cadet! To avoid this, my hand had to be up and away from the touchpad at all times while typing. The result was not good for me. I am hoping that this won't affect you like it did me! I feel I have to put this as a strong warning, as everyone types a little different. 
I mentioned earlier that this chromebook is very smooth, almost slippery. The bottom has this bumby, small rolling feel that has a unique feel I was not expecting. Who knows, maybe it's good for stress while writing that paper? :D 
The weight is pretty good for a 15” screen chromebook. Very light and small, letting it fit in practically any bag or backpack, which I feel goes well with the aesthetic of the whole device as a college device or school. The speed is definitely a highlight here. The i5 processor makes for very quick response time on apps to launch and just overall use with no lag! The intel graphics chip is fine for movies to stream, websites etc. At most, light gaming is passable here but nothing too demanding for sure. There is a selection of games in the market to check out.
The Google market for chromebooks for apps is much smaller compared to the Android market for phones for example.The apps I found were primarily for productivity apps for AI related jobs or productivity in general. As usual for Google products, this Lenovo chromebook comes with Gemini for AI related tasks. 
There is much to like about this chromebook this year. The many advancements in tech is a very welcome addition, as seen in the speed in this device. The oversized keyboard is a real killer for me as I will most likely need to use my usual kb with it. The $1100 price is high in my opinion, but if these descriptions are all highlights for you, then jump right in. *My advice is to try it out if possible before buying to make sure it is comfortable for you.* I personally can’t recommend this, but again, try it out and see if the keyboard doesn't sway you from buying it.
